items.stem: Which is capital expenditure?
options: The cost of installing a new machine
items.answer: The cost of installing a new machine
items.markingKey: The cost of installing a new machine. Installation is part of the cost of bringing the asset into use [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Capital expenditure is spending on acquiring or improving non-current assets that benefit several years; revenue expenditure is spending on running the business or maintaining assets, which benefits only the current period.
items.markingKey: Capital – acquire/improve NCA, long-term benefit [1]; revenue – running costs/maintenance, current period [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is important to distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Misclassification misstates profit and the value of non-current assets: capital expenditure written off understates profit and assets; revenue expenditure capitalised overstates both.
items.markingKey: Effect on profit [1]; effect on SFP/assets [1] [2]

items.stem: During the year Mekong Rice Mills spent the following amounts: delivery charge on new office equipment $500, legal fees on the purchase of premises $15,000, fuel for the delivery van $550, annual servicing of machinery $2,100. Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Capital $15,500; revenue $2,650
items.markingKey: delivery charge on new office equipment: capital; legal fees on the purchase of premises: capital; fuel for the delivery van: revenue; annual servicing of machinery: revenue [3]; totals capital $15,500, revenue $2,650 [1] [4]

items.stem: During the year Nile Valley Dairy spent the following amounts: electricity for the shop $2,200, cost of installing a new machine $1,850, redecorating the showroom $3,700, legal fees on the purchase of premises $18,250, repairs to the delivery van $1,350. Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Capital $20,100; revenue $7,250
items.markingKey: electricity for the shop: revenue; cost of installing a new machine: capital; redecorating the showroom: revenue; legal fees on the purchase of premises: capital; repairs to the delivery van: revenue [4]; totals capital $20,100, revenue $7,250 [1] [5]

items.stem: During the year Lagoon Boatworks spent the following amounts: repairs to the delivery van $1,850, fuel for the delivery van $800, redecorating the showroom $950, delivery charge on new office equipment $8,050, building an extension to the warehouse $6,500, purchase of a computer system for the office $4,150. (a) Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure. (b) Discuss why the owner of Lagoon Boatworks might be tempted to treat repairs as capital expenditure.
items.answer: (a) Capital $18,700; revenue $3,600 (b) It would raise reported profit (e.g. to impress a bank) but breaks the accruals/prudence concepts and overstates assets.
items.markingKey: (a) repairs to the delivery van: revenue; fuel for the delivery van: revenue; redecorating the showroom: revenue; delivery charge on new office equipment: capital; building an extension to the warehouse: capital; purchase of a computer system for the office: capital [5]; totals capital $18,700, revenue $3,600 [1] [6] (b) Higher profit/assets [1]; misleading – breaks concepts [1]; judgement [1] [3]

items.stem: During the year Orchid Pharmacy spent the following amounts: building an extension to the warehouse $12,350, purchase of a new delivery van $18,800, repairs to the delivery van $2,600, road tax for the delivery van $400. items.answer: The repairs to the delivery van is revenue expenditure – it maintains or runs the business and benefits only this period. Correct total capital expenditure: $31,150.
items.markingKey: Error: the repairs to the delivery van is revenue expenditure – it maintains or runs the business and benefits only this period [1]; correct total capital expenditure: $31,150 [1] [2]

items.stem: Complete the statement: Cost of sales is calculated as …
options: opening inventory + purchases − carriage outwards + closing inventory
opening inventory + purchases (net of returns) + carriage inwards − closing inventory
items.answer: opening inventory + purchases (net of returns) + carriage inwards − closing inventory
items.markingKey: opening inventory + purchases (net of returns) + carriage inwards − closing inventory. Carriage inwards is part of the cost of goods [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between gross profit and profit for the year.
items.answer: Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales (profit on trading); profit for the year is gross profit plus other income less all expenses.
items.markingKey: GP = revenue − cost of sales [1]; profit for the year after expenses and other income [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why carriage inwards is included in cost of sales but carriage outwards is not.
items.answer: Carriage inwards is part of the cost of getting goods into the business ready for sale; carriage outwards is a cost of delivering goods to customers, a distribution expense.
items.markingKey: Inwards – cost of acquiring goods [1]; outwards – selling/distribution expense [1] [2]

Inventory at 31 December was valued at $8,140. (a) Calculate the gross profit. (b) Calculate the gross margin, to one decimal place.
Explain why closing inventory is deducted in calculating cost of sales.
items.answer: Goods still unsold at the year end have not been sold, so their cost is carried forward to match against next year's revenue (accruals concept).
items.markingKey: Unsold goods not part of cost of sales [1]; matched with later revenue [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between non-current assets and current assets.
items.answer: Non-current assets are held for use in the business for more than one year (e.g. premises); current assets are held for less than a year and change constantly (e.g. inventory, receivables, cash).
items.markingKey: NCA – long-term use [1]; CA – short-term, circulating [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is important for a business to have sufficient working capital.
items.answer: To pay its current liabilities as they fall due and to finance day-to-day operations; too little may lead to inability to pay suppliers and loss of credit.
items.markingKey: Pay short-term debts [1]; consequence of shortage [1] [2]

items.answer: a non-current liability

items.answer: current assets minus current liabilities
items.markingKey: current assets minus current liabilities. Also called net current assets [1]

items.stem: Complete the statement: Goods taken by the owner for personal use are recorded by …
items.answer: debiting drawings and crediting purchases
items.markingKey: debiting drawings and crediting purchases. At cost, reducing purchases [1]

items.stem: Explain why drawings are not an expense of the business.
items.answer: Drawings are withdrawals of resources by the owner for private use; they do not help to earn revenue, so they reduce capital, not profit.
items.markingKey: Private use – not to earn revenue [1]; reduce capital not profit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why goods taken for own use are credited to purchases rather than sales.
items.answer: The goods are taken at cost and were never sold, so purchases are reduced to show the cost of goods actually available for sale.
items.markingKey: Not a sale/at cost [1]; reduces cost of goods for resale [1] [2]

items.stem: During the year Atlas Engineering spent the following amounts: legal fees on the purchase of premises $9,850, delivery charge on new office equipment $10,100, repairs to the delivery van $3,900, insurance of the premises $2,050, electricity for the shop $650. The bookkeeper included the repairs to the delivery van ($3,900) in capital expenditure, giving $23,850. Explain the error and calculate the correct total capital expenditure, showing your working.
items.answer: The repairs to the delivery van is revenue expenditure – it maintains or runs the business and benefits only this period. Correct total capital expenditure: $19,950.
items.markingKey: Error explained: the repairs to the delivery van is revenue expenditure – it maintains or runs the business and benefits only this period [1]; working: $9,850 + $10,100 [1]; correct total capital expenditure: $19,950 [1] [3]

items.stem: During the year Tundra Outdoor spent the following amounts: fuel for the delivery van $500, purchase of a new delivery van $19,700, redecorating the showroom $300, cost of installing a new machine $7,000. Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Capital $26,700; revenue $800
items.markingKey: fuel for the delivery van: revenue; purchase of a new delivery van: capital; redecorating the showroom: revenue; cost of installing a new machine: capital [3]; totals capital $26,700, revenue $800 [1] [4]

items.stem: During the year Orchid Pharmacy spent the following amounts: purchase of a computer system for the office $5,950, repairs to the delivery van $800, redecorating the showroom $2,600, legal fees on the purchase of premises $17,600, insurance of the premises $2,900, cost of installing a new machine $10,250, wages of sales staff $1,200. (a) Calculate the total capital expenditure and the total revenue expenditure. (b) The purchase of a computer system for the office was debited to an expense account. State the effect of this error on profit for the year and on non-current assets.
items.answer: (a) Capital $33,800; revenue $7,500 (b) Profit understated by $5,950; non-current assets understated by $5,950 (ignoring depreciation).
items.markingKey: (a) purchase of a computer system for the office: capital; repairs to the delivery van: revenue; redecorating the showroom: revenue; legal fees on the purchase of premises: capital; insurance of the premises: revenue; cost of installing a new machine: capital; wages of sales staff: revenue [6]; totals capital $33,800, revenue $7,500 [1] [7] (b) Profit understated $5,950 [1]; non-current assets understated [1] [2]

items.stem: Revenue $90,000, cost of sales $54,000, expenses $21,000. What is the profit for the year?

The following balances were taken from the books of Kilimanjaro Coffee for the year ended 30 June: sales $236,400, sales returns $1,150, inventory at 1 January $15,230, purchases $111,270, purchases returns $1,560, carriage inwards $450, wages $16,620, rent and rates $10,910, carriage outwards $2,410, discounts allowed $1,040, general expenses $5,970, discounts received $370, rent received $2,890. Closing inventory was $5,910. The bookkeeper calculated the gross profit as $116,220. Explain why this is wrong and determine the correct gross profit.
items.answer: Carriage inwards was deducted below gross profit instead of in cost of sales. Correct gross profit: $115,770.
items.markingKey: Error explained: carriage inwards was deducted below gross profit instead of in cost of sales [1]; working: $15,230 + $111,270 − $1,560 + $450 − $5,910 = $119,480 [1]; correct gross profit: $115,770 [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego owns Atlas Engineering. For the year ended 31 December the following figures are available: sales $203,800, sales returns $760, inventory at 1 January $17,690, purchases $100,660, wages $15,050, rent and rates $6,080, carriage outwards $710, discounts allowed $900. Inventory at 31 December was valued at $15,990. Calculate the gross profit.

The following balances relate to Cedar Hardware at 31 December: Inventory $7,200, Bank loan repayable in 2032 $44,900, Cash in hand $1,700, Accrued wages $500, Trade payables $2,800, Premises $128,000. The owner calculated working capital as $12,200. State the mistake made and give the correct working capital.
items.answer: Current liabilities were added to current assets instead of being deducted. Correct working capital: $5,600.
items.markingKey: Error: current liabilities were added to current assets instead of being deducted [1]; correct working capital: $5,600 [1] [2]

items.stem: The following balances relate to Andes Supplies at 31 December: Prepaid insurance $2,500, Bank loan repayable in 2032 $27,200, Trade payables $14,600, Motor vehicles (carrying amount) $11,000, Inventory $19,300, Premises $55,500. The bookkeeper calculated working capital as $36,400. State the mistake made and give the correct working capital.
items.answer: Current liabilities were added to current assets instead of being deducted. Correct working capital: $7,200.
items.markingKey: Error: current liabilities were added to current assets instead of being deducted [1]; correct working capital: $7,200 [1] [2]

items.stem: The following balances relate to Kilimanjaro Coffee at 31 December: Fixtures and fittings (carrying amount) $86,600, Inventory $18,900, Trade payables $5,600, Premises $48,400, Motor vehicles (carrying amount) $36,700, Cash in hand $1,200. Calculate the total of the current assets and the total of the current liabilities.
items.answer: Current assets $20,100; current liabilities $5,600

items.stem: The following balances relate to Zambezi Timber at 31 December: Trade receivables $9,800, Fixtures and fittings (carrying amount) $39,700, Premises $43,600, Trade payables $10,200, Bank overdraft $8,100, Inventory $6,800, Cash in hand $500, Accrued wages $1,800, Bank loan repayable in 2032 $45,300. (a) Calculate the total of the current assets and the total of the current liabilities. (b) Assess whether Zambezi Timber has a satisfactory level of working capital.
items.answer: (a) Current assets $17,100; current liabilities $20,100 (b) Compare current assets with current liabilities: a ratio around 1.5–2:1 is usually comfortable; too much may mean idle resources, too little risks paying debts.

items.stem: Mohammed owns Baobab Furnishings. At the year end the business had: motor vehicles (carrying amount) $16,700, prepaid insurance $1,600, fixtures and fittings (carrying amount) $81,000, trade payables $3,100, trade receivables $2,200, bank overdraft $10,600, premises $61,200, inventory $12,700, bank loan repayable in 2032 $31,000. (a) Calculate the total of the current assets and the total of the current liabilities. (b) Calculate the owner's capital (net assets) at the year end.
items.answer: (a) Current assets $16,500; current liabilities $13,700 (b) $130,700
items.markingKey: (a) CA: Prepaid insurance, Trade receivables, Inventory = $16,500 [1]; CL: Trade payables, Bank overdraft = $13,700 [1] [2] (b) NCA $158,900 + CA $16,500 − CL $13,700 − NCL $31,000 = $130,700 [2]

items.stem: Jonas, the owner of Silk Route Textiles, had capital of $50,700 on 1 January. During the year withdrew $10,480 in cash and took goods costing $1,100 for personal use. The business made a profit of $28,670 for the year. A trainee accountant calculated closing capital as $69,990. State the mistake made and give the correct closing capital.
items.answer: The goods taken for own use were added to capital instead of being treated as drawings. Correct closing capital: $67,790.
items.markingKey: Error: the goods taken for own use were added to capital instead of being treated as drawings [1]; correct closing capital: $67,790 [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila, the owner of Fjord Fisheries, had capital of $91,000 on 1 January. During the year withdrew $21,780 in cash and took goods costing $540 for personal use. The business made a profit of $39,110 for the year. Prepare the capital account (or calculate the closing capital) at 31 December.

Kenji, the owner of Harbour Electrics, had capital of $117,500 on 1 January. During the year Kenji paid in additional capital of $8,200, withdrew $21,750 in cash and took goods costing $1,960 for personal use. The business made a profit of $33,760 for the year. Prepare the capital account (or calculate the closing capital) at 31 December.
